prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of the optical lattice clock, based on trapping atoms at a magic wavelength, which brought atomic frequency standards to the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: a single-part prize to Katori and Ye for the optical lattice clock. After reading the full first round and the chair's summary, the committee is split four to four between B022 and B039, and I do not treat that count as an argument. The argument is the one our statutes ask for: an original experiment, verified by others, with the right people identified. Katori proposed the magic-wavelength lattice, which removes Doppler, recoil and light-shift limits at the same time, and demonstrated it. Ye's group then took it to the 10^-18 regime and showed what the lattice makes possible, namely many atoms interrogated at once and many-body effects inside the clock. The performance has been reproduced at RIKEN/Tokyo, JILA, PTB, NIST and SYRTE, and the clocks now resolve gravitational redshift over millimetres and constrain drifting constants and dark-matter couplings. That answers the chair's question about what the clock has delivered beyond a smaller error bar: these are measurements that could not be made before the door was opened. The credit is two named people and I can say who did the original work. On the chair's question about the SI second, I regard the redefinition as a consequence of the result and not a condition for it. For the citation, I would name the magic-wavelength lattice explicitly and state the 10^-18 level, which keeps it clearly apart from the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 prize for control of single quantum systems. Of the two names, I consider both essential: Katori for the concept and first realisation, Ye for taking it to record accuracy and for the work that made the many-body regime visible. Dropping either would misstate who did what. I did not change my preferred configuration; what moved is my confidence that B039 is the right second choice if the external checks disappoint on B022, and I keep B035 as the other alternative.
statement.case_against: The precedent question is still the real reservation and I do not think it can be argued away completely. Precision timekeeping has been recognised in 2005 and 2012, and a sceptical reader may say the lattice clock is an excellent refinement of a recognised lineage rather than a discovery about nature. My answer is that the lattice idea is a separate original invention, not a later and more elegant version of an earlier one, and that the physics it has opened is new, but this remains a committee judgement. The Lemonde, Ludlow, Hinkley and Hollberg contributions and the ion-clock groups are outside the two names, and none of us has verified the priority chronology among Sr, Yb and Hg lattice work. Finally, B039 is a strong alternative: the Kane-Mele Z2 idea and the HgTe observation are real discoveries with independent confirmation. My objection there is not importance but that I cannot yet be absolutely sure the trio identifies those who did the original work, given the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal and the separate 3D discovery.

responses.point: Eriksson argues that B039 has the broadest support, a clean theory-then-experiment loop, and that the Kane, Mele and Molenkamp trio is the most coherent set within the supplied names, with the citation covering the effect and topological insulators.
responses.response: I accept that the loop is closed and that the Z2 invariant is a real organising idea, and I would not oppose B039 if the committee chooses it. But your wording, prediction and experimental discovery of the quantum spin Hall effect and topological insulators, is exactly where my doubt sits. The 2D effect and the 3D materials are separate discoveries made by different people, and a citation that spans both implies credit for 3D work that Kane, Mele and Molenkamp did not perform. Danielsson's narrower wording, confined to 2D and HgTe, is the only version I could support, and then the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal stays outside the names. By comparison B022 has no such gap in its credited names, which is why I keep it first.

responses.point: Danielsson asks what new fact about nature the optical lattice clock has delivered beyond a smaller error bar, and ranked it only sixth because it looks like a metrology refinement.
responses.response: It is a fair challenge, and I answer with measurements and not with the error bar alone. Clocks at the 10^-18 level resolve the gravitational redshift across millimetres, which turns a relativistic effect into something measured inside a single sample. They also place limits on drifting constants and on dark-matter couplings, and the interacting-atom clock work is a many-body result. I take the earlier worry about the SI second as a separate issue. If the committee decides that none of this counts as discovery, then B022 should lose, and I would accept that. I do not think the record supports that conclusion, and I note that you place B022 as your first alternative to B039.

responses.point: Johansson notes that B039 and B022 together name five people, so a combined prize would need a subset of three, and she is wary of the pending SI second redefinition as an external driver.
responses.response: I agree that a two-part prize would not fit the limit without dropping a name from the clean B022 pair or from the B039 trio, and I would not break up either credit to create a combination. Each should stand as its own single-part case, and I would rather the committee decide between them on scientific grounds. On the SI second, I share your caution about outside decisions driving ours, which is why I say the result stands on the independent 10^-18 comparisons already made, and the redefinition would follow from it and not the other way round.

responses.point: Lindroth asks whether both Katori's early strontium demonstration and Ye's accuracy record are needed for a two-name credit, and notes that the lattice clock cuts against her taste for the unexpected.
responses.response: I think both are needed. Katori's contribution is the idea and its first realisation, and without it there is no magic-wavelength lattice. Ye's group demonstrated that the idea delivers record accuracy, and their many-body and comparison work is what turned it into a tool for fundamental physics. I accept your point that the clock is not an unexpected discovery in the way a new particle would be, but the statutes cover invention as well, and the original idea here is localised and verified. I would be content for the final citation to carry your wording on new tests of fundamental physics.

responses.point: Mehlig says B022 would win if precision were weighted above novelty, and raises the overlap with the 2005 and 2012 prizes against it.
responses.response: I think that framing of precision against novelty is slightly off, because the lattice is itself a new idea and not only a better number. I value novelty of concept, and the magic-wavelength trap is one. I agree that the overlap with earlier prizes must be addressed in the wording and not assumed away, which is why I want the citation to name the magic-wavelength lattice and not generic precision timekeeping. If the committee finds that overlap too heavy, my fallback is B039 with Danielsson's narrower citation, and I would want external views on priority before we vote.

uncertainties: Whether the 2005 and 2012 precedents leave room for a further precision-timekeeping prize remains a committee judgement.
Priority among Sr, Yb and Hg lattice work and the roles of Lemonde, Ludlow, Hinkley and Hollberg are not verified by me; external expert views would help.
For B039, whether the credit for the 2D effect can be separated from the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal and from the 3D work within three names.
For B035, whether the pairing mechanism must be settled before recognition; I keep it only as an alternative.
statement.conflict_note: No change. I have long-running microscopy exchanges with Tokyo and other Japanese groups, but no collaboration or personal tie to Katori or Ye, and I see no need for recusal on B022. Johansson is a Chalmers colleague, relevant only to B023, which I am not proposing. I have no connection to the B039 candidates.
